newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Two parties dominate final battle for Algeria votes.
newsitem.headline: Two parties dominate final battle for Algeria votes.

text.p: Five years after their previous free parliamentary election was cancelled, Algerians vote again on Thursday under the eyes of 200,000 armed security forces.
More than 60,000 people have been killed in sectarian violence since 1992, when voting was annulled with the radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) far in the lead.

As campaigning entered its final stretch on Sunday before the two-day compulsory "cooling off" period ahead of the vote, analysts said the main battle was between backers of President Liamine Zeroual and those of the Islamist-oriented party of Mahfoud Nahnah.

With 39 parties in the field, the race for first place in the next parliament was between the pro-Zeroual National Democratic Rally (RND) and Nahnah's former Hamas party, now called Movement for a Peaceful Society (MPS).
The election is being held out as proof of Zeroual's commitment to take this North African country of 29 million people to democracy after the failure of its first attempt.
The FIS is banned, but the shadow of Islamic radicalism and the years of bloodshed have weighed heavily on this campaign.
Among the thousands of victims, whole village communities have been almost wiped out in overnight raids which started late last year; even children have not been spared from having their throats cut.

And on Saturday, in a savage reminder of the constant threat of violence, a home-made bomb ripped through a cinema in central Algiers. L'Authentique newspaper said on Sunday that one moviegoer was killed and 24 wounded. Officials said earlier that five people were hurt.

Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia, a candidate under the RND flag in Algiers, lashed out at Nahnah saying he had paved the way for Moslem guerrillas who are slaughtering innocent people. Ouyahia was referring to Nahnah's past as a Moslem rebel involved in sabotage of power pylons to protest at the country's then one-party socialist state.

Analysts say Nahnah is the main challenge to the secularist parties. He and his party are scrupulously abiding by the new election law which bans the use of Islam to attract votes but his opponents believe a fundamentalist wolf lurks behind the moderate face of his movement.
He also took nearly one third of the votes in Algeria's first multi-candidate presidential election, won by Zeroual with more than 60 percent, in November 1995.
"We said nothing in 1995 (about alleged cheating in the poll) but in 1997 we will sweep everything," MPS supporters chanted at a rally on Saturday in the garrison town of Blida.
Nahnah's supporters already term him "the President" as they believe he will become Algeria's head of state in the next poll by the year 2000.
Election laws have been changed to rule out groups based on regionalism or language and more than 20 of the parties which took part in the 1991 general election have disappeared.

Parties need to gain five percent of the votes to be represented in the 380-seat National Assembly (lower house), and some, like the formerly ruling National Liberation Front (FLN), the Socialist Forces Front (FFS), and the Rally for Culture and Democracy (RCD), are expected to see their leaders easily elected.
But other parties could fall below the vote threshold and vanish.

For the past two weeks, political leaders have criss-crossed Algeria, a country five times the size of France, vowing to create jobs for more than 2.5 million unemployed, improve government management and bring peace and security to end five years of civil strife.

"The poll campaign was turned into a market of promises. We are not here to distribute promises," said Ouyahia, urging people to work hard for solidarity, justice and better management of the country's resources.
Modest turnouts at rallies by opposition leaders in their traditional strongholds showed the uphill struggle many face to secure their positions in Algeria's changing political map.
